headline: AI rewrites Bun 1.4 with 1M+ lines of Rust code, signaling the end of manual programming
summary: The massive AI-assisted rewrite of Bun from Zig to Rust, involving over 1 million new lines of code, suggests a future where AI agents generate most software, shifting human roles to reviewing outcomes rather than code.
details: The recent Bun 1.4 release featured a monumental rewrite from Zig to Rust, incorporating over 1 million new lines of Rust code. This was achieved largely through AI agents, a process that cost approximately $165,000 in API tokens over 11 days.

This unprecedented scale of AI-driven development suggests a fundamental shift in programming. The article posits that the era of humans manually writing and reviewing every line of code for useful software is nearing its end.

While this shift may lead to a surge of less refined software, it will also produce well-engineered solutions to real problems. Much of this software will function effectively without detailed human code review.

Evidence for this trend is seen in GitHub's exponential growth in code production since last year. This increase is theorized to come from side projects and internal company initiatives, not yet critical business products.

The Bun rewrite was spearheaded by Jarred Sumner, who used a pre-release version of Fable 5 with an unlimited token budget. He established the framework for multiple agents to work in parallel, translating the Zig codebase.

Over 11 days, these agents generated 6,778 commits, demonstrating the immense throughput possible. The initial revelation of the rewrite showed a change of +1,009,257 -4,024 lines, astounding the programming community.

The fact that AI produced over a million lines of reliable code, now running on millions of developer machines, is significant. Even with an 'oracle' for comparison, the ability to build and refine complex software through AI is a game-changer.

Developers at companies like Anthropic and OpenAI are reportedly shipping dozens or hundreds of pull requests weekly. This indicates a shift to higher-level system building, moving away from granular code review.
